UTZ $UTZ JUMPED $6.61 IN ONE SESSION. SIX WEEKS ADDED $0.15:

The name that does not lead a board is usually the more interesting read, because the argument is still open. Six companies below, one per Len5. The snack company that opens this note is the exception: its argument closed on a Tuesday, and four cents is what is left.

Utz Brands UTZ at $14.21, -$0.01 / -0.07% on Friday. The Hanover, Pennsylvania company makes salty snacks under Utz, Zapp's, Boulder Canyon and On The Border. The Momentum Len5 is watching it, and the verdict is this - the climb that put it here happened in a single session, and the six weeks since have been the stock sitting on a cash offer.

July 20 it closed $7.45. July 21, Intersnack Group of Germany agreed to pay $14.25 a share in cash, a 91% premium, in a deal valued at about $2.9 billion including debt. The Rice and Lissette families keep half; Intersnack takes the other half. Utz closed $14.06 that afternoon, +$6.61 / +88.7%, on 61.8 million shares against 1.7 million the day before.

Friday's $14.21 is $0.04 / 0.3% under the offer and $0.06 under the $14.27 high of August 25. From August 5: +$0.09 / +0.6%. That is the flat month. From June 5: +$7.14 / +101%, which is the same Tuesday wearing a three-month label.

The snack business did not double. Quarter ended June 28, reported August 5, with no earnings call: net sales $371.8M, +1.4%; branded salty-snacks organic sales - those brands after stripping acquisitions and currency - +3.3%; adjusted profit $0.19 a share against about $0.18 expected; adjusted EBITDA - profit before interest, tax, depreciation and some one-time items - $55.7M, +14.4%. Reported net income was a $16.0M loss. It was already the deal.

This Len5 looks for a price near its twelve-month best with the short and long windows pointing the same way. The long windows agree because of July 21. The short window is the offer. Pulse Biosciences at $53.24, -$1.47 / -2.69% on Friday, which makes devices doctors use to treat tissue with electrical pulses, sits on this same Momentum Len5 as the name still climbing.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: a break. The Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period - the time U.S. antitrust reviewers get to look at a deal before it can close - is expected to expire at 11:59pm ET Wednesday, September 9. The shareholder vote still required, including a majority of votes from shareholders outside the family group, has not been dated; a preliminary proxy went out August 24 with the meeting day still blank. Closing is mapped for the fourth quarter. If the deal fails, $14.21 is not a snack-business price.

Verdict: a 91% cash offer did the momentum work in one session, and four cents plus a dated antitrust clock is the whole remaining case.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
- Visa at $375.07, -$3.68 / -0.97% on Friday. It runs the network that moves money between banks when a card is tapped; it neither lends nor issues the cards. This Len5 wants a business hard to copy at a fair price, and only the price half is open. June quarter, reported July 28: net revenue $11.6B, +14%; processed transactions 71.7B, +10%; adjusted profit $3.32 a share. Visa bought 14.5 million of its own shares that quarter at an average $330.71 - $4.9B. Friday is 13.4% above that receipt, $10.50 / 2.7% under the $385.57 high of August 26. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: a real fall while volume keeps compounding. Results are not dated; last year's fourth-quarter print landed October 28. Verdict: nothing wrong with the network, and its own purchase receipts say the price has run.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
- Copart at $33.72, +$0.14 / +0.42% on Friday. The Dallas company runs salvage auctions for wrecked cars off yards that need land, zoning and a town willing to host a wrecking lot. This Len5 wants a good business priced under what it looks worth after something visible went wrong. The yards are the hard-to-copy half; Friday is $15.44 / 31.4% under the $49.16 high of September 8, 2025. Quarter ended April 30, reported May 21: revenue $1.24B, +2.1%; profit $0.43 a share against $0.42; cash and short-term securities $4.2B and no borrowings. Average selling prices +4.6% more than offset a 2.4% drop in units. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the fiscal-year print due Thursday, September 10 after the close - whether U.S. insurance units are still shrinking. Verdict: a permitted-land network with a full cash pile, marked down a third on slower wreck volume.

GROWTH LEN5:
- BOK Financial at $136.70, -$0.65 / -0.47% on Friday. The Tulsa, Oklahoma parent of BOKF, N.A. lends across the Southwest. This Len5 wants expansion nobody is overpaying for. July 20: profit $176.5M, or $2.92 a share against $2.19 a year earlier; strip a $30.9M one-time gain on swapping a block of Visa shares and a bond-repositioning loss, and it is $2.59, +18%. Loans $27.1B, +$896M / +3.4% from March, its strongest loan quarter on record, and it now maps full-year loan growth above 10%. Friday is about 12.9 times the $10.61 earned over the last four quarters. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: that loan pace fading, or credit costs arriving after two quarters of zero provision and $0.5M of net charge-offs. Next print is not dated; last year's landed October 20. Verdict: double-digit loan growth at thirteen times earnings.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
- AppLovin at $320.56, +$6.98 / +2.23% on Friday. The Palo Alto company sells software that places mobile ads in front of the people most likely to tap them. This Len5 wants a business still early as well as still fast. Fast is dated: quarter ended June 30, reported August 5, revenue $1.92B, +53%; net income $1.27B, about 66 cents of every sales dollar; adjusted EBITDA $1.61B at an 84% margin; free cash flow - cash left after running the business and buying equipment - $863M. Sequential growth was only +4% - the early half is the open question at this size - and from that August 5 close of $417.80 the shares are -$97.24 / -23.3%. The map for the quarter running now is $2.055B-$2.085B of revenue, 46% to 48% growth. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: that map printing, or sequential growth staying in the low single digits. Next results are not dated. Verdict: 53% on a nearly $2B quarter is still fast; the price already docked the slower step.

INCOME LEN5:
- Global Ship Lease at $46.40, +$0.66 / +1.44% on Friday. The Athens-based company owns container ships and rents them out on multi-year charters. This Len5 watches cash genuinely reaching owners and funded by the business. The dividend is $2.50 a year, paid $0.625 on September 3, about 5.4% of Friday's price, against $10.25 of profit per share over the last four quarters - a 24% payout. June quarter, reported August 5: operating revenue $198.7M; profit $89.3M, or $2.48 a share; 100% of 2026 days booked and 90% of 2027; $3.2B of contracted revenue. It ordered 15 new mid-size ships for $1.33B, more than 75% of that price covered by the first charters. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: coverage slipping, or the $2.50 coming down to fund the newbuilds. Next results are not dated. Verdict: a covered payout at a quarter of earnings, with the fleet already rented through next year.

Second place is supposed to be where the argument still lives. On Utz the argument lived on July 21, closed that afternoon, and left four cents and a Wednesday night clock.

Not investment advice.

text:
【意外と知らない｜英語で表現したい日本 ㊱ ― 「鏡開き」の鏡は mirror ではない】

正月が明けるころ。

神前や床の間に供えていた鏡餅を下げて、

割ったり、

小さくしたり、

お汁粉や雑煮などにして食べる。

これが、

「鏡開き」。

外国人から、

“What does kagami biraki mean?”

と聞かれたら、少し説明が必要です。

まず困るのが、

「鏡」。

mirror

ですよね。

でも鏡開きで開くのは、

鏡そのものではありません。

ここで大切なのは、

日本語の文字を一つずつ直訳しないこと。

鏡開きは英語なら、

Kagami biraki is a Japanese New Year tradition in which decorated rice cakes are taken down and eaten after being offered for the New Year.

「鏡開きとは、正月に供えていた鏡餅を下げて食べる日本の正月行事です」

くらいから説明できます。

ここで覚えたいのが、

take down

です。

「取り外す」
「下ろす」。
take down a decoration

「飾りを外す」

take down a sign

「看板を下ろす」

take down the New Year decorations

「正月飾りを下げる」

季節行事を説明するとき、とても便利です。

では、

鏡餅

はどう説明するでしょう。

英語では、

kagami mochi

と日本語を残し、

round rice cakes offered as New Year decorations

のように説明できます。

たとえば、

Kagami mochi consists of round rice cakes traditionally displayed as part of Japanese New Year celebrations.

「鏡餅は、日本の正月行事で伝統的に飾られる丸い餅です」

ここで、

consist of ...

も覚えておきたい。

「～から成る」。

The decoration consists of two rice cakes.

「その飾りは二つの餅から成っています」

The meal consists of several small dishes.

「その食事はいくつかの小皿料理から成っています」

構造を説明するときに便利です。

ではなぜ、

「鏡」

なのでしょう。

鏡餅の丸い形が、昔の丸い鏡を連想させることと関係しています。

英語なら、

The round shape is traditionally associated with old-style mirrors.

「その丸い形は、昔の鏡と伝統的に結びつけられています」

と言えます。

ここで再び、

be associated with ...

が使えます。

文化説明では本当によく使う表現です。

そして、

「開き」。

鏡開きでは、

餅を切る

というより、

割る

という表現が伝統的に好まれます。

英語では、

break the rice cakes into smaller pieces

「餅を小さく割る」

と説明できます。

ここで、

break A into pieces

です。

「Aを細かく割る」。

Break the chocolate into pieces.

「チョコレートを小さく割ります」

Break the rice cake into smaller pieces.

「餅を小さく割ります」

非常に実用的です。

そして鏡開きの面白いところは、

「open」

と訳したくなるのに、

実際には何かの蓋を開けるわけではないこと。

つまり、

open

ではなく、

break

のほうが具体的な動作として伝わりやすい。

これも英語表現の大切なポイントです。

日本語の名称は象徴的。

英語の説明は具体的。

この違いを使い分ける。

たとえば、

The word biraki literally suggests “opening,” but in practice the rice cakes are broken into pieces and eaten.

「biraki という語は文字通りには『開く』ことを示しますが、実際には餅を割って食べます」

と説明できます。

ここで、

in practice

も便利です。

「実際には」。

In theory ...

「理論上は」

In practice ...

「実際には」

文化や制度を説明するときに使えます。

そして鏡開きでは、

食べること

までが大切です。

単に飾りを片付けて終わりではない。

供えていたものをいただく。

そこで、

The rice cakes are then eaten, often in dishes such as ozoni or sweet red-bean soup.

「その後、餅は雑煮やお汁粉などにして食べられます」

と言えます。

ここで、

such as ...

「～のような」。

examples を出すときの基本表現です。

日本文化を説明するとき、

何でも細かく定義しようとすると長くなります。

そんなとき、

such as

で代表例だけ出す。

これで十分です。

さらに注意したいのが、

「鏡開き」の日。

地域や慣習によって違いがあります。

だから、

Kagami biraki is always held on January ...

のように一つの日付で断定するより、

The date varies depending on the region and tradition.

「日付は地域や慣習によって異なります」

と説明するほうが安全です。

ここでも、

vary depending on ...

です。

The date varies depending on the region.

「日付は地域によって異なります」

The custom varies by area.

「習慣は地域によって異なります」

日本文化は全国一律ではありません。

英語で説明するとき、

地域差を残しておくことも大切です。

外国人に鏡開きを簡単に説明するなら、

Kagami biraki is a Japanese New Year custom. We take down the kagami mochi, break it into smaller pieces, and eat it.

これだけでも十分です。

そして、

“Why is it called kagami?”

と聞かれたら、

Because the round rice cakes are traditionally associated with old-style mirrors.

と続ければいい。

ここで重要なのは、

鏡開き

という日本語を、

mirror opening

と無理やり英語にしないこと。

英語で文化を説明するときは、

名前の直訳

より、

実際に何をするか

を優先する。

What is it?

正月行事。

What do people use?

鏡餅。

What do they do?

下げる。

割る。

食べる。

Why is it called kagami?

丸い形と鏡の関係。

When?

正月後。ただし地域差あり。

この順番で考えれば、

take down

consist of

be associated with

break into pieces

in practice

vary depending on

という英語が一つの行事から学べます。

そして鏡開きは、

英語学習の面白い問題を一つ教えてくれます。

言葉の名前と、

実際の行動は、

必ずしも一致しない。

だから、

字面だけを訳すと不思議な英語になる。

文化を英語にするなら、

文字を見るだけではなく、

人が何をしているのかを見る。

鏡開きは、

mirror を開く行事ではありません。

餅を割り、

それを食べ、

正月の一区切りをつける行事です。

名前から入って、

動作まで説明する。

そこまでできれば、

日本文化はぐっと伝わりやすくなります。

是非フォローお願いします！

# Finding True Balance: A Family Provider’s Reflections on Rest, Work, and the Markets

In the fast-moving world of prediction markets, every decision carries weight. Yet as September 2026 unfolds and conversations about work-life balance dominate timelines, I’m reminded that sustainable success isn’t found in constant motion. It’s found in deliberate pauses. As a prediction market analyst covering Polymarket and Kalshi by day and a dedicated family provider on weekends, I’ve learned that real balance isn’t a perk—it’s a discipline.

This weekend, let’s step away from charts and probabilities to explore what genuine equilibrium looks like in both professional and personal life.

## The Myth of “Flexible Hours” and the Reality of True Balance

A recent discussion making waves on X cut straight to the heart of the issue. Many so-called flexible arrangements still expect late-night Zooms or quick replies during family time. True balance, the post argued, looks different: bosses who actively encourage early sign-offs, protect family hours, and respect full disconnection after the workday ends.

I’ve seen this play out in my own circle. Colleagues who treat evenings and weekends as sacred recover faster and return with sharper insights. In prediction markets, where edge comes from clear thinking rather than raw hours, this distinction matters. The traders who consistently outperform aren’t the ones glued to their screens 24/7; they’re the ones who know when to close the laptop and recharge.

## Gen Z’s Stand and the Shifting Expectations of Employers

Another trending conversation centers on Gen Z’s refusal to trade work-life balance for job security. A Times of India piece highlighted how younger professionals are pushing back against the old “grind now, live later” model, forcing employers to rethink what they offer.

This shift isn’t just generational noise—it’s a market signal. Companies that fail to adapt risk losing talent to those that prioritize sustainable rhythms. For analysts like me, the lesson is clear: the same principle applies to self-employment. If I overcommit during the week, my weekend recovery suffers, and so does my ability to read markets accurately on Monday.

As a family provider, I feel this tension acutely. My children don’t care about Polymarket volumes or Kalshi resolution odds. They care that Dad is present—physically and mentally—when it matters.

## Leadership, AI, and the New Perks That Actually Matter

Lighthearted takes about AI “learning work-life balance first” aside, serious leadership discussions are elevating balance as a core talent attractor. Forward-thinking managers now list genuine downtime support alongside compensation in job postings.

In prediction markets, where information edges can evaporate overnight, mental freshness is a competitive advantage. I’ve started treating rest as seriously as I treat research. That means no market checks after 8 p.m. on weekdays and full weekends reserved for family. The result? Better pattern recognition, calmer risk assessment, and more meaningful time at home.

## Life as a Family Provider: Why Rest Is Non-Negotiable

Weekends for me aren’t about catching up on work—they’re about being the provider my family needs. That includes emotional presence, not just financial stability. When I protect my rest, I show up as a better husband and father. The motivational reminder I return to often is simple: “You cannot pour from an empty cup.” Markets will always be there. Childhood moments won’t.

Another quote I keep close: “Rest is not idleness; it is the foundation of effective action.” In a field obsessed with probabilities and edge, this truth is easy to forget until burnout forces the lesson.

## Practical Steps Toward Sustainable Balance

- Set non-negotiable offline hours and communicate them clearly.
- Use weekends to model healthy boundaries for your family rather than catching up on tasks.
- View rest as an investment in long-term performance, not a luxury.
- Revisit your definition of success: Is it endless output, or consistent, high-quality contribution over decades?

## Conclusion: Markets Reward the Balanced Mind

Prediction markets teach us to price probabilities accurately. Life teaches us that the highest probability of long-term success belongs to those who protect their energy. As we head into another week of analyzing Polymarket and Kalshi outcomes, I’m carrying this weekend’s lesson forward: the best traders—and the best providers—know when to step away.

Rest well. The markets, and your family, will be waiting when you return refreshed.

🔥 CyberForge CVE of the Day #043

🚨 CVE-2026-85046 — Chrome V8 Type Confusion Under Active Exploitation

Google has patched a High-severity type-confusion vulnerability in Chrome’s V8 JavaScript and WebAssembly engine—and confirmed that an exploit already exists in the wild.

CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue one day after public disclosure.

This is not merely an interesting compiler bug or a theoretical browser crash. Crafted JavaScript delivered through a webpage can corrupt V8’s understanding of an array’s element type and ultimately produce arbitrary code execution inside Chrome’s renderer sandbox.

The essential boundary must nevertheless remain clear:

⚠️ CVE-2026-85046 provides sandboxed renderer execution. It does not independently guarantee complete operating-system compromise.

A separate sandbox escape or equivalent security failure would normally be required for full host control. That does not make the vulnerability routine—a dependable renderer primitive is often the indispensable first stage of a complete browser exploit chain.

🔑 Key details:

⭐ Severity: High
📊 CVSS v3.1: 8.8
🧮 Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
🧠 Weakness: CWE-843 — Type Confusion
🎯 Target: Google Chrome / Chromium V8
🌐 Attack vector: Network
⚙️ Attack complexity: Low
🔓 Authentication: None
👆 User interaction: Required—the victim must render attacker-controlled web content
⚔️ Confirmed impact: Arbitrary code execution inside the renderer sandbox
🚨 Exploitation: Confirmed in the wild by Google
📋 CISA KEV: Listed 4 September 2026
⏰ Federal remediation deadline: 18 September 2026
🧪 Public research: Trigger, root cause and heap-exploitation primitives published
🛡️ Chrome fix: 152.0.7977.82/.83 on Windows and macOS; 152.0.7977.82 on Linux
🔄 Restart required: Yes—the fixed browser must be relaunched

🧬 What actually went wrong?

V8 stores metadata describing the type of values held inside a JavaScript array.
An array containing small integers can be represented as PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS, while an array containing objects uses a more general representation such as PACKED_ELEMENTS.
These distinctions allow V8’s Maglev and TurboFan compilers to generate faster specialised code. The optimisation remains safe only while the compiler’s assumptions match the array’s real contents.
For selected small arrays, V8 introduced an optimisation that could inline Array.prototype.sort rather than repeatedly moving between built-in and JavaScript comparison functions.
Conceptually, V8 performed the following operations:

1️⃣ Check the receiver array and its expected maps.

2️⃣ Copy the elements into a temporary snapshot.

3️⃣ Sort that snapshot while calling the supplied JavaScript comparison function.

4️⃣ Recheck the original receiver after the comparator’s side effects.

5️⃣ Copy the sorted snapshot back into the original array.

The temporary copy is deliberate. JavaScript comparison functions can have side effects—including modifying the array being sorted.
The flaw lived in the post-comparison safety check.
Instead of proving that the receiver retained the exact element type associated with the temporary snapshot, the optimiser accepted any map previously observed by the function.
An attacker could train the function with both object arrays and small-integer arrays. They could then begin the vulnerable operation using an array of object references and use the comparator to replace every element with an integer.

Because Array.prototype.fill() can replace every element in place, V8 may migrate the receiver backwards from the general object-elements map to the specialised small-integer map without allocating an entirely new backing store.

The faulty check sees a map it already knows and allows execution to continue.

V8 then copies the temporary object references back into an array now labelled as containing small integers.

The result is an impossible internal state:

🔹 The array metadata says “small integers.”
🔹 The backing slots contain tagged object pointers.
🔹 Different engine operations interpret the same bits differently.

That is the type confusion at the heart of CVE-2026-85046.

🧪 Why the confusion is exploitable:

The discoverer’s technical analysis demonstrates two particularly useful consequences.

First, operations that trust the false small-integer map can expose object references as integer-like values. This supplies an address-disclosure primitive and helps an exploit defeat uncertainty about the JavaScript heap layout.

Second, operations performed under the false assumption that the array contains only integers may omit the garbage collector’s write barrier.

Write barriers tell the garbage collector when an older object begins referencing a younger object. If V8 moves an object pointer while treating it as an integer, it may fail to record that relationship.

With controlled allocations and garbage collection, the attacker can create a stale reference and reclaim the underlying memory with attacker-arranged data. That supports construction of a fake JavaScript object.

Address disclosure and fake-object capability can then be developed into arbitrary read/write access within the JavaScript heap. From there, an experienced browser exploit developer can manipulate V8 structures and obtain native execution in the renderer context.

The researcher reports chaining the flaw with an n-day sandbox escape during a V8 CTF exercise. That demonstrates chainability in a research environment.

It does not establish that the same sandbox escape was used in the attacks Google observed.

⚔️ The practical attack chain:

1️⃣ An attacker creates a malicious page containing JavaScript designed to exercise the vulnerable sorting optimisation.

2️⃣ The victim reaches the content through phishing, malicious advertising, a redirect chain, a compromised legitimate site or ordinary browsing.

3️⃣ Chrome executes the JavaScript inside a renderer process. The attacker needs no account on the device or browser.

4️⃣ Repeated calls provide compiler feedback involving both packed object and small-integer arrays.

5️⃣ V8 optimises the affected sorting function.

6️⃣ During sorting, the attacker-controlled comparator changes the receiver array’s element type while the temporary snapshot still contains object pointers.

7️⃣ The insufficient map check accepts the altered element type.

8️⃣ V8 copies object pointers into an array marked as containing small integers.

9️⃣ The attacker converts the type confusion into address disclosure and JavaScript-heap manipulation.

🔟 Successful exploitation yields arbitrary code execution inside the renderer sandbox.

1️⃣1️⃣ Conditional second stage: the attacker uses a separate sandbox escape, privilege escalation or serious policy failure to reach the wider operating system.

1️⃣2️⃣ Only after that wider compromise can conventional post-exploitation actions—payload delivery, credential theft, persistence or lateral movement—follow.

🌍 Why this matters operationally

The browser is designed to process untrusted content continuously. A victim does not need to download and deliberately run a conventional executable.

The vulnerable engine may be reached through:

🔹 A phishing or messaging link
🔹 A malicious advertisement
🔹 A compromised legitimate website
🔹 A watering-hole page
🔹 An attacker-controlled site
🔹 A redirect or traffic-distribution chain
🔹 An application embedding an affected Chromium runtime

Browsers also sit beside high-value authenticated sessions: email, identity services, cloud consoles, financial systems, source-control platforms and administrative interfaces.

Renderer execution does not automatically expose every browser secret, especially while Site Isolation and sandbox boundaries hold. But it gives an attacker a powerful position from which to attack adjacent boundaries or combine the bug with a second exploit.

The modest early EPSS score must not distort prioritisation. EPSS is a statistical estimate—not a verdict on whether exploitation has occurred. Google has already confirmed exploitation, and CISA has already placed the vulnerability in KEV.

Direct evidence outranks an early probability model.

🛡️ Affected and fixed software:

🔴 Google Chrome for Windows before 152.0.7977.82
✅ Fixed in 152.0.7977.82/.83 or later

🔴 Google Chrome for macOS before 152.0.7977.82
✅ Fixed in 152.0.7977.82/.83 or later

🔴 Google Chrome for Linux before 152.0.7977.82
✅ Fixed in 152.0.7977.82 or later

Microsoft confirms that Edge Stable 152.0.4191.62 incorporates the Chromium fix. Administrators should install the newest Stable release offered rather than stopping at a historical minimum.

Other Chromium-based products—including Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, Electron applications, Chromium Embedded Framework and distribution-supplied Chromium packages—must be evaluated through their own vendor releases.

Chrome and Edge version numbers are not directly interchangeable. Sharing Chromium code does not mean products share build numbers or identical release schedules.

Google’s cited release is a desktop advisory. It should not be stretched into an undocumented mobile version matrix.

🔄 Do not forget the restart

A downloaded browser update does not replace code inside an already running vulnerable process.

After updating Chrome:

✅ Fully relaunch the browser
✅ Check chrome://version or chrome://settings/help
✅ Verify the running build—not merely the package staged on disk
✅ Recheck endpoints where users can indefinitely postpone restarts

🔎 Defender hunting guide
No authoritative campaign domains, JavaScript signatures or complete in-the-wild exploit samples have been published. Detection must combine inventory, browsing telemetry, crash evidence and post-exploitation behaviour.

1️⃣ Find vulnerable and pending-restart browsers
Query endpoint management, software inventory and Chrome Enterprise reporting for builds below 152.0.7977.82.
Include dormant laptops, virtual desktops, kiosks, developer systems, privileged-access workstations, jump hosts and unmanaged devices connecting to organisational services.
Find machines where a fixed package has been installed but an older browser process remains alive.

2️⃣ Review renderer instability with context

Search Chrome crash reports, Windows Error Reporting, macOS diagnostic reports and Linux crash telemetry for unusual renderer failures around suspicious navigation.

Look for several users crashing after visiting the same domain or redirect chain.

A crash alone is weak evidence: ordinary websites, extensions and graphics drivers also cause renderer failures, while a polished exploit may avoid crashing.

3️⃣ Hunt abnormal process relationships

Investigate cases where Chrome or a related renderer/utility process is followed by unexpected execution of:

🔍 PowerShell
🔍 cmd.exe
🔍 wscript.exe or cscript.exe
🔍 mshta.exe
🔍 rundll32.exe or regsvr32.exe
🔍 Shell interpreters
🔍 curl or wget

Also examine executable or script creation in temporary, cache, profile or startup locations; process injection; browser credential-store access; security-tool interference; new persistence; and unexpected outbound traffic from browser child processes.

These are exploit-chain indicators, not unique signatures for CVE-2026-85046.

4️⃣ Correlate web and endpoint evidence

Preserve DNS, proxy, secure-web-gateway, email-click and browser-history telemetry covering the vulnerable period.
Correlate suspicious navigation with renderer crashes, EDR events, file writes, child processes and authentication anomalies.

Do not automatically trust a legitimate domain. Watering-hole attacks deliberately use compromised sites that victims already recognise.

5️⃣ Search for downstream impact

If wider endpoint compromise is suspected, examine:

🔍 Browser-cookie and credential database access
🔍 Theft or replay of cloud, email or administrative sessions
🔍 Suspicious OAuth grants
🔍 New sign-ins following the browser event
🔍 Payload staging and outbound transfer
🔍 Persistence or lateral movement from the affected identity

🚑 Defensive action:

✅ Update Chrome immediately
✅ Relaunch and confirm the running version
✅ Update Edge to the newest offered Stable release
✅ Inventory other Chromium browsers and embedded runtimes separately
✅ Prioritise administrators, developers, finance users and cloud operators
✅ Enforce short forced-relaunch windows for emergency browser releases
✅ Use least privilege and application control
✅ Separate high-value administration from general web browsing
✅ Preserve telemetry covering the vulnerable browsing window
✅ Hunt for browser-to-host transitions rather than relying on a universal JavaScript signature

If exploitation is suspected, isolate the endpoint while preserving volatile evidence. Capture process trees, network connections, browser and OS crash artefacts, relevant memory where policy permits, browsing records and secure-web-gateway telemetry.

Determine the last time a vulnerable browser processed untrusted content and the first confirmed execution of the repaired build.
Investigate credential and session exposure. Changing a password alone may not invalidate a stolen browser session token; explicit session revocation may be required.
Where host-level compromise cannot be confidently excluded, rebuild from a trusted source.

🧾 Evidence separation:

Confirmed by Google and official records: V8 type confusion, crafted-HTML delivery, sandboxed arbitrary code execution, affected version boundary, fixed Stable builds, reporter and active exploitation.

Confirmed by CISA: KEV addition, remediation deadline and active-exploitation prioritisation.

Confirmed by Microsoft: Edge released a Stable build incorporating the Chromium fix.

Confirmed by the discoverer: the vulnerable small-array sorting optimisation, mixed element-kind failure, address disclosure, skipped write barrier, arbitrary JavaScript-heap read/write path and source-level fix.

CyberForge interpretation: Public technical detail lowers the barrier for additional exploit development. Confirmed exploitation and KEV status outweigh the modest early EPSS probability.

Not established: the responsible actor, victim set, delivery infrastructure, campaign IOCs, mass exploitation, ransomware involvement or the sandbox escape used during real attacks.

🔥 CyberForge verdict:

CVE-2026-85046 is exactly the sort of vulnerability for which severity, exploit evidence and practical exposure align.

It is High rather than Critical. User interaction is required. The confirmed execution boundary is the renderer sandbox.

None of those facts makes it routine.

A hostile page can reach the vulnerable engine during normal browsing. The attacker needs no account. Google confirms an exploit exists in the wild, CISA has placed it in KEV, and the discoverer has explained how a subtle compiler mistake becomes a potent heap-corruption primitive.

The defensive verdict is:

🚨 Patch and relaunch immediately, then hunt selectively across the vulnerable browsing window.
Version compliance is the most dependable immediate control. Detection cannot rely on a public JavaScript signature because authoritative campaign indicators have not been released and exploit code can be transformed.
Prioritise vulnerable browsers used for identity, administration, finance, development and access to sensitive cloud services. Treat uncertain update or relaunch compliance as urgent. Continue retrospective hunting even after the repaired browser is running.
The one-sentence CyberForge verdict:
An actively exploited browser-engine zero-day with public heap primitives is an emergency update, even though full host compromise still requires the attacker to cross a second sandbox boundary.

15 July 2021
Holly Honderich
BBC News, Washington
The discovery in May of the evidence of remains of 215 Indigenous children - students of Canada's largest residential school - prompted national outrage and calls for further searches of unmarked graves.

Since then, more unmarked gravesites have been found, providing previews of investigations by Canada's First Nations into the deaths of residential school students.

A rising tally of these graves - more than 1,100 so far - has triggered a national reckoning over Canada's legacy of residential schools. These government-funded boarding schools were part of policy to attempt to assimilate Indigenous children and destroy Indigenous cultures and languages.

Here's what we know about the findings so far.

What do we know about the 215 graves?
In May, Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc Chief Rosanne Casimir announced that the remains of 215 children had been found near the city of Kamloops in southern British Columbia (BC) as part of a preliminary investigation.

Some of remains are believed to be of children as young as three.

All of the children are believed to have been students at the Kamloops Indian Residential School - the largest such institution in Canada's residential school system.

The remains had been confirmed with the help of ground-penetrating radar technology, Chief Casimir said, following preliminary work on identifying the burial sites in the early 2000s.

The full report into the remains found is due on Thursday, and the earlier findings may be revised. Indigenous leaders and advocates have said they expect the 215 figure to rise.

"Regrettably, we know that many more children are unaccounted for," said Chief Casimir in a statement.

Thousands of children died in residential schools and their bodies rarely returned home. Many were buried in neglected graves.

To this day there is no full picture of the number of children who died in residential schools, the circumstances of their deaths, or where they are buried. Efforts like those of the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc First Nation and others are helping to piece some of that history together.

The Kamloops school, which operated between 1890 and 1969, held up to 500 Indigenous students at any one time, many sent to live at the school hundreds of kilometres from their families. Between 1969 and 1978, it was used as a residence for students attending local day schools.

Of the remains found, 50 children are believed to have already been identified, said Stephanie Scott, executive director of the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation. Their deaths, where known, range from 1900 to 1971.

But for the other 165, there are no available records to mark their identities. Children "ended up in pauper graves," Ms Scott said. "Unmarked, unknown."

What about the other sites?
In June, the Cowessess First Nation in Saskatchewan announced it had found an estimated 751 unmarked graves after a similar investigation - the largest such discovery to date. The remains were found near the former Marieval Indian Residential School, which operated from 1899 to the 1990s and under the control of the Roman Catholic Church for much of that time.

Cowessess leaders have not yet determined if all the unmarked graves belonged to former students. Technical teams will continue the investigation to provide verified numbers.

Cowessess Chief Cadmus Delorme emphasised that the discovery was of unmarked graves - not a mass grave site - and suggested that the Catholic Church may have removed grave markers at some point in the 1960s.

A week later, the Lower Kootenay Band in British Columbia said the remains of an additional 182 people had been found near the grounds of the former St Eugene's Mission School. St Eugene's was operated by the Catholic Church from 1912 until the early 1970s.

"No reconciliation without truth": A survivor recounts abuse in Canadian residential school
And in mid-July, the Penelakut Tribe in British Columbia said it had identified some 160 "undocumented and unmarked graves" on their grounds and foreshore near the former site of the Kuper Island Industrial School. They offered few details, though the tribe has been working with researchers in recent years to find potential gravesites.

Giving a voice to missing and murdered women
What are residential schools?
The Kamloops residential school was one of more than 130 others like it. The schools were operated in Canada between 1874 and 1996.

A linchpin in the government's policy of forced assimilation, some 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were taken from their families during this period and placed in state-run boarding schools.

The policy traumatised generations of Indigenous children, who were forced to abandon their native languages, speak English or French and convert to Christianity.

Christian churches were essential in the founding and operation of the schools. The Roman Catholic Church in particular was responsible for operating up to 70% of residential schools, according to the Indian Residential School Survivors Society.

"It was our government's policy to 'get rid of the Indian' in the child," said former National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations Perry Bellegarde. "It was a breakdown of self, the breakdown of family, community and nation."

1883
Canada’s first prime minister, Sir John A Macdonald, authorises the creation of a residential school system, established by Christian churches and the federal government, with the intent to assimilate indigenous peoples in Canada.

Children in a residential school dormitory in the 1950s
Image captionChildren in a residential school dormitory in the 1950sImage copyright byGetty Images
1960s
The residential school system begins to wind down - though the last school will close in 1996 - as the psychological and cultural impacts of the schools come under growing scrutiny.

An estimated 6,000 children die at the schools, according to the former chair of Canada’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission Murray Sinclair. They die from causes like disease, neglect, or accidents. Physical and sexual abuse is also common.

There is still no full picture of the number of children who died or where many of them are buried.

2008
Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper issues a formal apology for the residential school system, which saw over 130 such institutions operating across Canada.

“Today, we recognise that this policy of assimilation was wrong, has caused great harm, and has no place in our country,” he says.

Prime Minister Harper with Phil Fontaine, a Canadian Indigenous leader, in 2008
Image captionPrime Minister Harper with Phil Fontaine, a Canadian Indigenous leader, in 2008Image copyright byGetty Images
2015
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada releases its final report on the legacy of residential schools and describes the central policy behind the system as one of  “cultural genocide”. It recommends funding to find burial sites and commemorate the children who died away from home.

2021
Tk’emlúps te Secwe̓pemc First Nation in British Columbia announces that a preliminary investigation, using ground penetrating radar, has found an estimated 215 unmarked graves at the site of a former residential school. Other First Nations in Canada are conducting similar research.

A memorial near the spot where the remains of the children were discovered
Image captionA memorial near the spot where the remains of the children were discoveredImage copyright byGetty Images
The landmark Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) report, released in 2015, detailed sweeping failures in the care and safety of these children, and complicity by the church and government.

"Government, church and school officials were well aware of these failures and their impact on student health," the authors wrote. "If the question is, 'who knew what when?' the clear answer is: 'Everyone in authority at any point in the system's history.'"

Students were often housed in poorly built, poorly heated, and unsanitary facilities, the report said. Many lacked access to trained medical staff and were subject to harsh and often abusive punishment.

The squalid health conditions, the report said, were largely a function of the government's resolve to cut costs.

"We have records in our archives of school administrations arguing with the Indian affairs government at the time about who was going to pay for the funerals of students," Ms Scott said. "They would do it all at minimal expense."

What do we know about the search for missing children across Canada?
Research by the TRC found that thousands of Indigenous children sent to residential schools never made it home.

Physical and sexual abuse led some to run away. Others died of disease or by accident amid neglect. As late as 1945, the death rate for children at residential schools was nearly five times higher than that of other Canadian schoolchildren. In the 1960s, the rate was still double that of the general student population.

Getty Images Shoes, flowers, candles and signs are on the steps of the Metropolitan United Church. Indigenous youth are holding a sit in front of the Ryerson statue near Church and Gould on the Ryerson University campus.Getty Images
Children's shoes have been left at makeshift memorials across Canada
"Survivors talked about children who suddenly went missing. Some talked about children who went missing into mass burial sites," said former TRC chair Murray Sinclair in a statement in May.

Other survivors spoke of infants fathered by priests at the school, taken from their mothers at birth and thrown into furnaces, he said.

The TRC identified 3,200 confirmed deaths, though it noted that the work of identification and commemoration was "far from complete". Mr Murray estimated some 6,000 children may have died.

What has been done?
In 2015, the TRC issued 94 calls to action, including six recommendations regarding missing children and burial grounds. Prime Minister Trudeau promised to "fully implement" all of them.

According to a running count by the CBC, 10 of the projects have been completed, 64 are in progress and 20 have not begun
The TRC, struck in 2009, fought for the issue of unmarked burial sites to be included in its mandate
In 2019, the government committed C$33.8m ($28m; £19.8m) over three years to develop and maintain a school student death register and set up an online registry of residential school cemeteries
So far, the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation says it has received just a fraction of this money though "discussions are ongoing"

What has been the reaction?
In early July, Mr Trudeau visited Cowessess First Nation and said it was "shameful" that children died because of residential schools and the "legacy of inter-generational trauma" caused by the policy.

Ms Scott, along with Chief Bellegarde and other Indigenous leaders, have pressed the government for a thorough investigation of all 130 former school sites to find any unmarked graves.

"Trudeau has been willing to move on this, he's got a lot of words, but we really need to see action," said Ms Scott.

First Nations community members gather for a vigil in Marieval after a discovery of unmarked graves
The discoveries also cast a shadow over the country's 1 July Canada Day holiday. Municipalities across Canada called off celebrations this year in recognition of the findings.

The preliminary findings have also renewed demands for an apology from the Catholic Church - one of the calls to action in the TRC report.

In 2017, Mr Trudeau asked Pope Francis to apologise for the church's role in running Canada's residential schools - but the church has so far declined.

The United, Anglican and Presbyterian churches issued formal apologies in the 1980s and 1990s.

News of the BC discovery also spurred a global response, prompting statements from Human Rights Watch and the United Nations.

A RECORD LOAN QUARTER AT BOK FINANCIAL $BOKF, AND 33 CENTS OF THE PROFIT CAME FROM VISA:

BOK Financial BOKF at $136.70, -$0.65 / -0.47% on Friday. Six companies below, one per Len5, and not one is the name that usually gets the headline. That is the point: the name everybody leads with is the one whose argument is settled, and the one standing behind it is where the argument is still live. The Tulsa bank just produced the largest quarter of new lending in its history, and the reason its profit beat expectations had nothing to do with lending.

It is the parent of BOKF, N.A., lending to businesses and households across Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado and the rest of the Southwest. The quarter, reported July 20:

- Loans $27.1B, up $896M in three months: +3.4% on the quarter, +11.5% on the year, the largest single quarter of new loan production in company history
- Reported profit $176.5M, or $2.92 a share, against about $2.63 modeled
- Strip the one-time items - gains and costs that will not repeat - and it earned $2.59, a shade UNDER that estimate
- Fees and commissions, what it charges for services rather than earns on loans: $202.0M, DOWN $7.8M on the quarter

Those 33 cents have a name. On May 8, Visa at $375.07, -$3.68 / -0.97% on Friday, closed a swap offer letting banks trade the restricted stock they have held in it since its listing for shares they can eventually sell. BOK Financial was in that queue and booked a $30.9M pre-tax gain, net of the hedge against it. A real gain on a real asset, and one that happens once.

None of the $896M arrived by buying another bank, and management raised the full-year loan growth map above 10%. What went backwards is the half that makes this bank unusual. It runs a large trading and wealth operation, so fees matter more here than at most banks its size: trading fell $9.7M on disrupted markets and mortgage banking gave up $2M, swallowing a record quarter from the fiduciary and asset management arm.

The Growth Len5 is watching it, and that style wants expansion at a price nobody has already bid up. The expansion is dated, and it was won rather than bought. Price is the other half: $136.70 is about 12.9 times the $10.60 earned over the last four reported quarters, and $9.37 / 6.4% under the $146.07 close of August 14. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: loans holding that pace through a quarter with no share swap in it, and fees turning back up. BOK Financial has not dated the September quarter; calendars carry Wednesday, October 28.

Verdict: the lending is the engine, the beat was not, and 12.9 times earnings is the price of telling those apart.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
- Utz Brands at $14.21, -$0.01 / -0.07% on Friday. The Hanover, Pennsylvania company makes salty snacks. This Len5 wants a price near its twelve-month best with the short and long windows agreeing. They agree for two unrelated reasons: +101% over three months, from $7.07 on June 5, and +0.35% over one. On July 21 Intersnack Group, a family-owned German snack maker, agreed to buy every Class A share for $14.25 cash, a 91% premium. Friday is four cents under that. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: no shareholder meeting has been dated, and closing is mapped only to the fourth quarter. If it breaks, this business was worth $7.07 nine weeks ago. Verdict: the strongest quarter-long move here and the flattest month, both written by one contract.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
- Visa again, on the trait this style picked it for. It runs the network money crosses when a card is tapped, and neither lends nor issues the cards. This Len5 wants a business hard to copy at a price that does not assume everything goes right. Hard to copy is settled: the June quarter, reported July 28, put net revenue, what Visa keeps after paying banks and partners, at $11.6B, +14%, with payments volume past $4 trillion in one quarter for the first time. Price is the open half and the thinnest markdown here, $9.07 / 2.4% under the $384.14 of August 25 - in a quarter where money paid to its own clients rose 18% and costs 19%, both outrunning that 14%. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: those client payments growing slower than revenue again. Not dated; its financial year ends September 30. Verdict: the quality question closed years ago, and the price says so.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
- Copart at $33.72, +$0.14 / +0.42% on Friday. The Dallas company runs the online auctions where insurers sell off wrecked cars, from yards that need land, zoning and a town willing to host them. This Len5 wants a good business priced under what it looks worth after something visible went wrong. Something did: Friday is $15.18 / 31.0% under the $48.90 close of last September 11. The quarter ended April 30, reported May 21: revenue $1.24B, +2.1%; profit $0.43 a share. American insurance cars sold fell 4.2% while the average car fetched 4.1% more, a record for a third quarter. Fewer wrecks, dearer wrecks. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: whether American volumes are still shrinking. Copart said on September 1 that full-year results land after Thursday's close, September 10 - the only firm date on this board. Verdict: permitted yards marked down a third on a question answered in five days.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
- AppLovin at $320.56, +$6.98 / +2.23% on Friday. The Palo Alto company runs the software deciding which advertisement appears inside a phone game, and bills the advertiser. This Len5 wants a business still early as well as still fast. Fast is dated: the quarter ended June 30, reported August 5, put revenue at $1.92B, +53%, and net income at $1.27B - 66 cents kept out of every revenue dollar - on $869.0M of operating cash and $863.3M of free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and buying equipment. The $5.7M between those two figures is its entire equipment bill for the quarter. Early is the half leaving: its own map for the quarter now running is $2.055B-$2.085B, 46% to 48% growth, but only 7% to 8% above the quarter just reported. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: that sequential step. Not dated; the last landed August 5. Verdict: the cheapest growth to manufacture here, stepping down on the company's own numbers.

INCOME LEN5:
- Global Ship Lease at $46.40, +$0.66 / +1.44% on Friday, its highest close in twelve months. The Athens company owns mid-size container ships and rents them out on multi-year charters. This Len5 watches cash genuinely reaching owners and funded by the business. Both halves are dated to August 5: profit belonging to common holders $89.3M, or $2.48 a share in one quarter, against a dividend of $0.625 a quarter, $2.50 a year, near 5.4% of Friday's price. One quarter covers a full year of the payment, and every 2026 sailing day is already hired out, with 90% of 2027. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the shipyard. It has committed $1.33B for 15 new vessels arriving from late 2028, only a little over 75% of that covered by cash the first charters should produce. Not dated; the last landed August 5. Verdict: the best-covered payout here, now carrying a construction bill.

Five of these six still have something open - a price, a signature, a delivery date. BOK Financial's is arithmetic: $2.92 reported, $2.59 earned, $896M of new loans nobody had to buy. A bank that lent more in three months than ever before did not need a gain on a payment network to make the quarter read well. It got one anyway. In October it will not.

Thomas Kitchin’s “Mexico or New Spain” is one of the most popular maps depicting the American Southwest during the late 18th century.

Engraved by Kitchin to illustrate Dr. William Robertson’s History of America, the map appeared in numerous editions and languages over roughly 35 years, helping European readers visualize Spain’s vast North American possessions.

First published in 1777, it captures the state of European cartographic knowledge just before Jesuit exploration and the expansion into Upper California began producing more detailed geographic information.

The map provides particularly interesting detail in New Mexico and southern Arizona, while its depiction of Texas remains comparatively sparse—reflecting the limited information then available to European mapmakers.

Published in London in 1795 and hand-colored, this 15 × 11-inch map offers a fascinating window into how North America was understood and imagined in the late 18th century.

The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.

Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.

Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.

Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.

Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.

Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017. 

In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.

Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.

What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.

He Defended Faith and Family

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.

Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.

He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.

No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.

Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.

That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.

He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.

Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.

Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.

Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.

After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.

Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

On September 6, 1901, President William McKinley was mortally wounded at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, NY.

The previous day, McKinley had given a well-received speech at the Expo. So, despite his staff's concerns for his safety, he attended a public meet-and-greet the Temple of Music theater. The theater’s organist played a Bach sonata while visitors queued to meet the president.

When McKinley offered to shake his hand, Czolgosz shot him twice. One bullet ricocheted off a coat button, but the other ripped into the president's abdomen. McKinley staggered back, and "Big Jim" Parker, an Expo employee, punched Czolgosz, preventing him from firing again. Then the president's guards wrestled Czolgosz to the ground as McKinley implored them not to hurt him. 

Then McKinley's concern moved to his wife, Ida. He asked his personal secretary to be careful how he broke the news of the attack to her. 

McKinley was carried to the Expo’s hospital, where he had emergency surgery by a gynecologist, who was the only doctor available. Although the doctor was able to suture the wounds to the president's stomach, he couldn't find the bullet.

At first, McKinley seemed to be recovering well. Then gangrene formed, and he declined rapidly. A few hours before his death, he said, "It is useless, gentlemen. I think we ought to have prayer." His last words were "Good-bye; good-bye! It is God's will; his will be done, not ours. Nearer, my God to thee; e'en though it be a cross, is my constant prayer."

He died in the early hours of September 14th. He had been popular, so his assassination led to a great outpouring of grief. Entire cities ground to a halt as their citizens paid their respects when the president's funeral train slowly passed on its way to Canton, Ohio.

McKinley was the third president to be assassinated in office. This prompted Congress to expand the mandate of the Secret Service (which had been created by President Lincoln to combat counterfeiting) to protect the president 24/7.

In patterns of domestic abuse, the one with greater power fixates on the other’s flaws while refusing to examine their own behavior or impact. 

The same dynamic plays out at the scale of nations.

We spend enormous energy condemning other countries’ ambitions—Russia, governments labeled socialist or authoritarian—while rarely examining the costs of our own policies. 

Sanctions that quietly devastate civilian economies stay offstage. 

At home, debates rage over labels while most working people simply want fair wages, affordable health care, and a government that puts them ahead of corporate donors and defense contractors. 

Every major power pursues its interests. The question is whether America’s version still serves ordinary Americans.

The United States maintains the world’s largest network of overseas bases—roughly 750 sites in more than 80 countries. Places like Okinawa function as self-contained American communities far from home. 

Iraqi oil revenues have long moved through the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; recent actions have given Washington similar leverage over Venezuelan oil proceeds. 

These arrangements project power and lock us into permanent commitments that drain resources from problems here.

For decades, U.S. policy backed right-wing forces across Central and South America under the banners of anti-communism and the drug war. The result was not mere neglect of local interests—it was systematic terror, mass killings, disappearances, and the destruction of democratic possibilities for generations of ordinary people.

The human toll of the post-9/11 wars is staggering. Brown University’s Costs of War project counts 905,000–940,000 direct deaths and another 3.6–3.8 million indirect deaths—more than 4.5 million total. Earlier Lancet studies recorded massive excess mortality in Iraq. Sanctions have added further preventable deaths. 
Venezuela has seen direct U.S. intervention. In Syria, a group that evolved from an al-Qaeda affiliate now leads the interim government. Cuba and Iran remain under pressure. NATO continues to define a European front against Russia.

This is sustained by a bipartisan permanent war economy. One side prioritizes Europe; the other the Middle East. Both keep the machinery running. 

The result is continuity: 

endless commitments, trillions spent, and working families left to pay the bill.

America First means ending wars that do not make Americans safer or more prosperous. 

Standing against ethnic cleansing/genocide means applying the same standard everywhere. 

Prioritizing the working class over the corporate and military-industrial class means questioning an empire that serves neither.

History shows the pattern. During the Gilded Age and Great Depression, workers and farmers asked for fair wages, safer conditions, and basic security. 

Elites resisted or offered minimal concessions. 

The reforms that came—labor protections, Social Security, the right to organize—were forced by sustained pressure from below. 

Ordinary people had to keep organizing and fighting. 

Socialists and communists helped build the movements that made the status quo untenable. 

Meaningful change has never arrived by waiting for elites to decide the time is right. 

And when that pressure mounts, those in power will often deny the harm, attack the critics, and reverse the roles—claiming they are the real victims.

text: Stablecoins are supposed to simplify crypto. But look closer at today’s market mechanics, and you’ll find they’re quietly building a leverage loop that makes the last cycle look like a warm-up. The new trick? Stablecoin mortgages. You borrow dollars against your Bitcoin, but the lender isn't a bank—it's a protocol that mints another stablecoin to fund the loan. That new stablecoin gets deposited, rehypothecated, or used as collateral elsewhere. Suddenly, your Bitcoin isn't just backing one loan; it’s seeding a two-layer stack of debt that can unwind faster than anyone can type "liquidation." This isn't just clever engineering. It's a collateral velocity trap. When Bitcoin moves up, the loop feels great—borrow, mint, lend, repeat. But velocity cuts both ways. When price stalls or dips, the entire chain of collateral starts to shiver. The same Bitcoin that was once sitting safely in cold storage is now a keystone in a domino line. If that sounds familiar, it’s because we’ve been here before—just in a different costume. The 2012 Bitcoin ghost is haunting today’s institutional liquidity mirage. Back then, the fear was Mt. Gox and a handful of exchanges. Now, it’s the illusion that institutional custody and regulated futures make the system "safe." But institutions don’t remove risk; they concentrate it in new places. The liquidity looks deep until everyone tries to exit the same door at once. The ghost isn’t the code—it’s the behavior. It’s the assumption that price will always be there to bail you out. Take the recent $4.5 million recovery story. It sounds like a win—stolen funds clawed back. But peel the onion, and it exposes a systemic blind spot: collateral reuse. That Bitcoin was probably pledged, loaned, or tangled in a web of obligations that no one fully mapped. The recovery is great for the one victim, but it reveals how opaque the collateral layer has become. If one recovery takes months of forensic work, imagine what happens when thousands of positions need to be sorted out simultaneously. The blind spot isn’t the thief—it’s the architecture that lets collateral be in two places at once without anyone screaming. Now, zoom out to geopolitics. Stablecoin colonialism is a term that sounds harsh, but it’s accurate. Dollar pegs are reshaping Asia’s crypto sovereignty. Countries that once dreamed of independent digital currencies are now finding that their citizens prefer the stability of a dollar-backed token—even if it means ceding monetary policy to Washington by default. It’s not a military conquest; it’s a monetary one. And it’s happening quietly, one mobile wallet at a time. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s $1 million monthly scam leak is a grim but revealing data point. It maps Bitcoin’s true sell-side fault line. When scammers launder or offload funds, they create sell pressure that has nothing to do with market sentiment. That’s not a trader capitulating; that’s a criminal rotating assets. It means the "real" supply isn’t just miners or whales—it’s illicit flows that can hit exchanges at any hour, regardless of news cycles. The market keeps watching ETF flows, but the real fault line might be a scammer’s wallet in a war zone. Flip over to traditional markets, and the Fed is quietly rewriting the playbook. The data-center pivot is the sleeper story. The Fed’s attention is shifting toward the energy and infrastructure demands of AI and cloud computing. That means rural zoning boards—not just interest rate projections—are becoming the real transmission mechanism for policy. If data centers can’t get power, growth slows. If they can, inflation might creep in through an unexpected door. The next rate decision might matter less than a county planning meeting in Virginia or Texas. And if you think inflation is contained, look at sugar. The 2026 rally is shaping up to be the Fed’s new canary in the coal mine. Sugar isn’t just for your coffee—it’s in processed foods, ethanol, and global supply chains. When sugar prices spike, it’s a leading indicator that food inflation is coming down the pipe. The Fed watches core CPI, but the real world feels sugar, wheat, and energy. If sugar is rallying, the central bank’s "transitory" language is about to age poorly. Speaking of the Fed, the rate hike itself isn’t the shock anymore. The real story is the dollar’s new supply logic. It’s not just about the federal funds rate; it’s about how the dollar is created, circulated, and hoarded in a world of digital assets and shifting reserves. The old models of money supply don’t fit when stablecoins are minted offshore and treasuries are tokenized. The dollar’s strength isn’t just policy—it’s plumbing. History offers a grim mirror. The 1931 parallel is hard to ignore. Gold repatriation back then shattered the collateral assumptions of Europe and the EMEA region. Today, we’re seeing a similar recalibration—not with gold bars, but with energy collateral and digital assets. Europe’s energy collateral is draining northward, not eastward. That’s a counterintuitive flow. The narrative says energy goes to Asia or stays local. But the data suggests liquidity and collateral are consolidating in Northern Europe, leaving the periphery thinner and more fragile. And what about the Dutch central bank’s gold exit? It’s being read as crisis prep, but it’s actually a real-yield signal. When a conservative institution like DNB moves gold, it’s not fear—it’s math. They’re signaling that real yields in Europe are about to do something that makes gold less attractive relative to other assets. It’s a portfolio shift, not a panic button. So what does all this mean for the average reader? It means the old rules of thumb are breaking. Bitcoin isn’t just a hedge or a risk asset—it’s now a collateral engine with hidden gears. Stablecoins aren’t just on-ramps—they’re monetary policy tools that bypass central banks. And the Fed isn’t just watching jobs and prices—it’s watching power grids and sugar farms. The connective tissue between all these stories is leverage and collateral. Whether it’s Bitcoin-backed mortgages, gold repatriation, or energy flows, the market is being driven by who can pledge what, to whom, and at what speed. The winners will be those who understand that collateral isn’t static. It moves, it compounds, and sometimes, it vanishes. The takeaway? Don’t just watch the price. Watch what the price is built on. text:
Every evening across millions of Indian villages, a quiet public health crisis used to unfold inside humble kitchens.

A mother would bend down over a traditional mud chulha, blowing furiously into a hollow metal pipe (phukni) to keep wet firewood burning. The thick biomass smoke filled the unventilated room, exposing women and young children to severe, long term respiratory risks day after day.

It was a massive, stubborn challenge deeply rooted in poverty, fuel availability, and rural habits.

In the mid-2000s, an ambitious effort emerged to tackle this issue through advanced combustion science.

The core tech, a compact, forced-draft micro-gasifier, was engineered in collaboration with scientists at the prestigious IISc Bangalore, led by Prof. H.S. Mukunda, Dr. S. Dasappa, and their team.

Instead of burning wet wood, the stove used a small, battery operated fan to drive precise airflow through processed pellets made from agricultural waste like peanut shells and sugarcane bagasse. 

When operated correctly, it converted biomass into a cleaner, far more efficient blue flame.

This was not a tiny backyard experiment. It was initially incubated inside global energy major BP under its Emerging Consumer Markets division around 2006.

When BP later exited non core initiatives, Indian leaders Mahesh Yagnaraman and Mukund Deogaonkar, along with The Alchemists Ark, bought out the business and formed First Energy.

They launched the Oorja stove, embarking on the largest commercial rollout of gasifier cookstoves the world had ever seen, selling between 400,000 and 500,000 household units.

Yet, despite backing from a global corporate, patented world class Indian science, and massive field deployment, the household model hit a wall.

Independent field studies, including a landmark Stanford survey of nearly 1,000 households across Maharashtra and Karnataka, revealed a sobering truth: only a small fraction of buyers were still using the stove a few years after purchasing it.

Why did a venture with brilliant science and half a million units sold fail to stick in rural kitchens?

Because as every technopreneur eventually learns through blood and sweat: Designing an efficient hardware product is only 20% of the battle. The remaining 80% is the ruthless reality of last mile distribution and unit economics.

- Oorja’s bottleneck was the pellet.

- To keep the stove operational, a rural family needed an affordable, unbroken supply of agricultural pellets every single month. 

- Building a distributed network of pelletizing plants, sourcing raw crop waste seasonally, and delivering heavy bags across remote villages proved logistically overwhelming.

- As raw material and transport costs rose, pellet prices climbed. 

- Firewood remained "free" at the point of use for poorer households, while families who could afford convenience used Oorja merely as a secondary backup to LPG.

When fuel supply chains faltered, 100s of 1000s of stoves sat unused on kitchen shelves. Years later, the government's PM Ujjwala Yojana expanded LPG connections across rural India, making pellet dependent household stoves even harder to defend.

But First Energy did not simply vanish / fold....

Recognizing the failure of the household retail model, the management executed a sharp, pragmatic pivot: they moved away from home kitchens and redesigned Oorja as a commercial gasifier for restaurants, hotels, and caterers.

In commercial kitchens, unsubsidized LPG was expensive, and businesses had the scale and willingness to buy pellets in bulk. 

The pivot worked, industrial heating major Thermax later acquired a stake in the company in 2015 to take the Oorja commercial platform forward.

The story of Oorja offers one of the most vital case studies in Indian entrepreneurship.

It demonstrates that a product can feature patented science, sell nearly half a million units, and still fail its primary target audience if the surrounding supply chain cannot sustain the user's daily habits.

text:
Brian Chesky on the year Airbnb almost didn't exist:

Summer 2008. The company is two designers, an air mattress, and a name, Airbed and Breakfast that they will spend the next several months trying to convince anyone to take seriously.

They need $150,000. They're offering ten percent of the company at a $1.5 million valuation.

Chesky meets Michael Seibel, who tells him about a category of person he's never heard of:

"Michael Seibel says there are these people called angels and they'll give you money, and the first thing I thought is, I can't believe this guy believes in angels. That's how naive I was."

Seibel makes about 20 introductions. Angel investors and a couple of venture capitalists. Here is the entire outcome of that campaign, in Chesky's own accounting:

"About 10 to 12 or 13 probably didn't meet us. We probably met a half dozen people… Everyone ran away from the idea. No one funded us."

Why the market said no

The first objection was the founders themselves.

"Joe and I were designers, and as far as they were concerned, designers didn't start companies. We didn't look like a tech founder, which I think is ridiculous, because I don't think you should ever hire someone because they look like something else. You want a new thing? Well, maybe they'll look different."

The template on offer was narrow:

"If you didn't drop out of Harvard, or you didn't drop out of a PhD program at Stanford, well, you weren't going to be the next Google or Facebook."

Chesky's objection is that the template contradicted its own history "the previous tech company founders didn't drop out of Stanford. So it was a little absurd."

The second objection was the size of the thing. Investors asked how many air beds there are in the world, and the founders couldn't argue, because their own first deck built the total addressable market off airbed sales. Airbnb-as-we-know-it was, at that moment, a stray remark:

"One day somebody said, I want to rent my bedroom. And I said, well, all you have to do is get a mattress, inflate it… And I thought, at some point we should open the model up."

The third objection, "the bigger problem," in Chesky's words — was the premise:

"People did not think strangers would stay with other strangers. They thought it was crazy."

One investor said it to his face: "Brian, I hope that's not the only idea you're working on."

Then the macro finished the job. Late 2008, an investor tells them:
