They packed lunch, because they had already worked out how the day was going to end. Fifteen Black students spent a Tuesday morning in 1968 on the carpet of the University of Miami president's office, eating food from home and reading books, until the police came for them and one officer who had graduated from that same university walked over and asked Harold Long if he would get up and walk. Long smiled at him and stayed exactly where he was. He was risking a law school scholarship and he knew it.

Twenty six Coral Gables policemen had been on alert since Saturday, and their chief was standing on the University of Miami campus at seven in the morning.

They were there for fourteen Black students who wanted their university to teach the history of Black people in America, and who had asked in writing for a good deal more than that.

The students were members of United Black Students, which had won recognition on that campus the year before and was the first Black organization the university had ever had. They came up the stairs of the Ashe Administration Building at 8:47 on a Tuesday morning in May 1968 and walked into the second floor office of the president.

Twelve men and two women took the couches and the floor of the outer office.

Harold Long, who had founded United Black Students and was its president, asked whether Henry King Stanford would talk to them.

Bryce Dunham, an assistant to the president, told them it would have to be right then, because Stanford was booked for the rest of the day.

Long went in. He came back out about ten minutes later and told the others it was the same as it had been every other time, that the president would not make a commitment.

Harold Fields, the group's vice president, started to say that there was nothing else they could do but this, and did not finish the sentence.

So somebody turned on a radio in the outer office and ran it at almost full volume.

The president of the university asked them to turn it down, and a dean asked them to turn it down. Neither request worked.

That radio is the smallest thing in this story and the only thing in it that anybody had to invent on the spot. Everything else those students did that morning was procedure, and they had been following procedure for a month.

Procedure had gotten them one piece of paper with one word on it.

Long had been on that campus since 1964, when he enrolled as a freshman the same year the Civil Rights Act was signed. The university had been admitting Black students since the summer of 1961, when the Board of Trustees voted to accept qualified applicants regardless of race.

The first of them arrived by the dozen onto a campus that had thousands of students on it.

That vote is the story the university likes to tell. What the vote did not do was change a single line in the course catalogue.

That month of procedure had begun at a president's breakfast in April at which, by Stanford's own later account, nobody handed him a petition or a demand.

Five days after that breakfast, Dr. King was killed in Memphis. United Black Students organized the memorial service the university held on the ninth of April, and Stanford suspended classes after eleven that morning so people could attend.

There is a photograph from that service. Harold Long is speaking to the university on the Student Union patio with Stanford standing on one side of him and the director of the county's community relations board standing on the other.

Five weeks later the police would carry him down a staircase two hundred yards from that patio.

On the seventh of May the same students handed the president a typed document with ten items on it, called Program Objectives of Priority to be Submitted and Acted Upon by the University of Miami Administration.

They asked for recruitment of Black students, and for two hundred scholarships. They asked for courses in Afro American culture and background, for Black faculty to teach them, for Black speakers, for a stated minimum percentage of Black students on the campus, and for a security force that was not entirely white.

On the curriculum they were specific. Seven courses, and thirty new professors.

Stanford wrote to his department chairmen. He told them the curriculum belonged to them and not to him, that serious budget commitments were involved, and somewhere in that correspondence he used the word neo segregationist.

United Black Students read that word for exactly what it would do to a department chairman holding a memo from his president.

Fields, the group's vice president, answered it in print that same week, in the student paper. He wrote that the university already offered courses dealing with essentially every other ethnic and racial group in the country, and not one on African culture, on the history of the continent, or on the history of Black people in America.

He wrote that the administration was accusing the students of the precise thing the administration was doing. Denying people the knowledge of their own heritage, he wrote, is institutional discrimination.

Nobody added a course.

The Monday night before the sit in, the students met in an apartment belonging to one of the student newspaper's columnists and planned it, and by midnight the Coral Gables police knew it was coming.

By 9:20 on Tuesday morning there were fifteen students in the president's outer office. Some of them opened lunch bags they had brought from home.

Others read. They laughed, and talked, and after a while they sang.

The food was the tell. Nobody packs a lunch for a meeting they expect to last ten minutes.

Stanford came out and asked them into his office. Five went in and the rest stayed on the floor.

Father Gibson, one of Miami's Black civil rights leaders, came into the building and called members of the group out into the hall to talk them into leaving. Nobody left.

Then Stanford and William Butler, the vice president for student affairs, came into the reception area and asked the students whether they intended to stay.

The answer came back at them as one word from the whole room.

Stanford, with visible regret, asked Butler to read a prepared statement. It said that any student who refused to leave was subject to suspension or expulsion, and that the Coral Gables police would be asked to act.

Long answered him: "We will wait all day if we have to."

Butler read the statement twice more. The students sang a verse of something and then took up a line about going off to jail, and they kept singing it while a vice president stood in front of them holding a piece of paper.

Valveta Turner was one of the two women on that floor. She said she was willing to stay in jail until some kind soul got around to bailing her out.

She had been born and raised in Florida and had gone to all Black schools her whole life. Her mother worked from seven in the morning until midnight, and had worked as a maid in white homes.

She had never had any desire to go to a white school. She had applied late, would have preferred Temple, and took the first offer that came, which was this one.

She told the paper she would die for the cause, and the reporter wrote that what had happened to her family was what had brought her to it.

The other woman was Jackie Hawkins, and the university had made her one of its official hostesses.

She was a sophomore and an only child, and she lived with her grandmother in Winter Park. She was not there on scholarship, and she described her family as middle class and her neighborhood as not a good neighborhood but a Black one.

She had spent her entire education in mostly white schools, and she remembered teachers as well as students calling her names. She said the advice was always to ignore it, and that ignoring it only made them do it more.

She had read Stokely Carmichael and Malcolm X and called herself a believer in Black Power. She said she would burn down her own house if she thought it would help.

Asked about the civil rights workers she had admired as a child, she said she now thought they had been masochists, and that nonviolence had become a thing for the Black middle class.

That was the young woman the university had chosen to send out and greet its visitors.

Then the helmeted officers came into the outer office.

The police chief asked the students whether they were going to be gentlemen about it. Long told him that depended entirely on how they were treated.

The police decided they would take everybody except the two women, who were made to walk out under their own power.

One of the officers had graduated from that same university, and he came over and asked Long whether he would get up and walk.

Long smiled at him and did not move. He was picked up and carried out of the building, and the others went the same way, one at a time, down the front stairs of their own administration building while the rest of the student body stood and watched.

The paper's photographer caught five policemen carrying a student named Ralph Jones. The caption noted that a hundred and eighty five pounds of him would not stay off the ground and that he bounced down the stairs.

Outside, two men in the crowd were wearing guns. Reporters from the student paper walked up and asked whether they were FBI, and the men said no, and eventually said they were from Wackenhut, which is to say the university had private armed security standing on its lawn that morning.

At around ten past one, white students began picketing in front of the administration building with signs reading that the university had a racist system, and that it was not going to be a cool summer or a cool fall, it was now.

After two hours of marching there were about twenty five of them. When the television cameras arrived the number went up to thirty five.

Back in Coral Gables that morning, the booking had taken over an hour. The students were fingerprinted and photographed and put in the city jail.

Wilbur Johnson had a comment about the jail when he got out. It was segregated.

Johnson was twenty five, from Chester, Pennsylvania, and the paper called him the intellectual force behind United Black Students. He had started in an NAACP Youth Council that he and a friend eventually had to leave, because the two of them had gotten further out ahead of the branch than the branch was willing to go.

In 1961 he had ridden with the Philadelphia Friends on the Freedom Rides.

Seven years after riding a bus into the segregated South, he was sitting on the carpet of a Florida college president's office, and the country's answer to him had not changed enough to be worth measuring.

Eleven of the students were released on their own recognizance into the custody of local Black civic leaders. Father Gibson came down to post bond.

Long turned bond down at first and said he would stay in the cell. He reconsidered later.

There was a condition attached to their release, which was a promise not to encourage or instigate any further activity. The student paper reported that the promise was partially kept.

Long was an undergraduate with law school in front of him, and the paper noted that the morning had put his law school scholarship at risk. He had said there comes a time when you stand up for what you believe in, and asked what kind of man he would be, and what kind of lawyer, if he did not do it now.

Back on the campus, at a quarter to three that afternoon, Stanford called a press conference in the same building.

He said it was regrettable that the confrontation had left the university no recourse but the action it took. Asked whether the students would be suspended or expelled, he said Butler would consider their conduct and make recommendations, and that it would go through the usual disciplinary machinery.

Asked whether he had known it was coming, he said he generally knew what was going on around his campus.

Stanford's own record is the part of this that does not resolve.

He had come to Miami from Birmingham-Southern College, where by the student paper's account he refused to dismiss a Black student and the Klan burned a cross on his campus. As chairman of a regional accrediting commission he had wired the governor of Mississippi over the admission of James Meredith, telling Ross Barnett what would happen to the accreditation of every state institution in Mississippi if he did not stop.

In 1964 he was given a human relations award for advancing the cause of brotherhood in the South. Two years later he refused a request from the mayor of Miami to cancel a campus speech by Dr. King.

Four years after that award he had fourteen of his own students carried out of his office by police.

Within a week of the sit in the Board of Trustees approved twenty five scholarships for disadvantaged Black students, to be called the John F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King, Jr. Memorial Scholarships.

Twenty five, against the two hundred in the document.

A reporter reached Long for a reaction and got one that has aged better than anything else said that week. He called it a perpetuation of white superiority, and then he said that they were happy to have them.

Two departments agreed to add courses. Long said the group was scheduled to meet with five more within days and that the results so far were fairly encouraging.

Five months later the university printed its course bulletin for 1969 and 1970, and the Black oriented courses were not in it.

On the twenty ninth of October more than a hundred students tore the pages out of that bulletin and burned them in a trash can on campus.

A week after that, Long resigned as president of United Black Students.

The courses did come. In the spring of 1969 the university offered work on African economic development, on problems in sub Saharan Africa, on Black Americans in politics, and on the history of Black people in the United States, and United Black Students ran the first Black Culture Week that campus ever had.

In March 1969 there was another sit in at the Ashe Building. That December, ten members of United Black Students and three high school students were formally charged with disrupting school functions and unlawful assembly.

Through the 1970s the organization wrote and printed something called the Malaika handbooks, which were guides for the Black students coming in behind them on how to get through the place.

A Division of Afro American Studies was established in 1973, five years after the sit in.

A Center for Global Black Studies got its budget approved in 2021 and opened on the Coral Gables campus in February 2022, fifty four years after fifteen people sat down on a floor and demanded that Black studies have a place on that campus.

The building where students go for services now carries Harold Long's name. He died in February 2021, a practicing attorney in the city he had gone to jail in.

All of that commemoration carries the wrong date.

The university, its alumni magazine, its student paper and its own library timeline give the date of the sit in as the seventeenth of May, 1968. A Coral Gables magazine history published in 2025 gives the fourteenth, and almost nothing else does.

The seventeenth of May, 1968 was a Friday, and it is the date printed on the masthead of the newspaper that broke the story. The account inside that newspaper puts the sit in on the Tuesday, because the police knew about it Monday night, because the students' own review forum met that Tuesday evening to go over what had happened that morning, and because the caption under the photographs says Tuesday.

The Tuesday was the fourteenth.

The count is off as well.

The fifteenth person in that room was George Freeman Battle, a graduate assistant in the mathematics department, which is why he is the only one of them who was not an undergraduate. When the paper printed the names of everybody the police took out of that office, it printed fifteen.

Harold Long, Harold Fields, William L. Johnson, Wilbur Johnson, James Westley Thompson, John Samuel, Ralph Jones, Franklin Burton, Lynwood Johnson, Willard James Butler, Wayne Thompson, George Freeman Battle, Jackie Hawkins, Valveta Turner, and one more man who comes down to us as Reginald, because the rest of his name sits in a column of the scanned page that cannot be read.

Fourteen is the figure the university repeats every February.

Fifteen people were taken out of that office on a Tuesday. In the page that survives, one of them can still only be read as Reginald.

text:
Lieutenant General Raj Shukla (retd.) of the Indian Army appeared on an NDTV show today arguing that the Indian military is far behind in its thinking and needs a shakeup. I agree. However, in his enthusiasm the LTG gets a lot of important details very wrong. If these were trivial, it would be ok to ignore and move on. But he uses these facts as supporting evidence to make a very far-reaching case. With respect, I would like to offer a few observations and corrections.

The General says:

1. "Asim Munir has become Kissinger" pointing to the expanded diplomatic clout of Pakistan's Field Marshal. No counterpoints offered here - just an observation.
2. Silicon Valley VCs pick up the 12 brightest minds from Stanford and offer them $2B each before they even have an idea, in order to build defense systems. I don't know who has given the General this information. It is false.
3. China can build one billion drones a year. This is false.
4. The Russians prepared for years and then fielded a massive tank assault with Arena systems in the "Maya corridor" (I think he meant Mayak, in Donetsk) which was defeated in this mythic last-stand-of-the-tank type battle. The truth is this was a test involving a few Russian tanks that used the Arena system with 12 anti-drone interceptors each. The test showed the efficacy of this system with a high number of interceptions. It exposed issues with magazine depth, particularly magazine depth requirements / km of incursion in a heavily defended area. By most accounts seven tanks were lost. This was not a multi-year preparation, nor is this the tank's last stand, nor was this some huge last ditch tank believers v drone believers doctrinal struggle. It was exactly the opposite of what the General presented; tank adaptation.
5. Alex Karp of Palantir drove across Poland to see Zelensky, who refused, but eventually met him. Karp then said, take my software for free give me your data, and thus he created Palantir. False. Palantir was around for nearly twenty years prior to the Ukraine war even beginning.
6. Palmer Luckey was playing with VR headsets ten years prior to the Ukraine war. The CIA funded him and in five hundred and some days, he fielded the Fury unmanned CCA prototype. False. Luckey's Anduril bought Blue Force Technologies, which is where the Fury came from. Development on this concept started in 2019. That is seven years. (The 568-day figure is Anduril's later prototype-to-first-flight clock after that acquisition, not the birth of the aircraft. This marketing figure, which the General bought without investigating it, undercuts his "plane in no time" argument.)
7. Indian IT CEO said, give me $10B and I will get you to frontier AI in a year. Let's give him $10B. First, take that pitch with a datacenter full of salt. If someone says give me $10B and I'll get you to frontier AI in 12 months, that is not how frontier AI is built. There is nothing "false" about reporting that someone said it, but it does expose a very, shall we say, "innocent" way of thinking.
8. "If we had Claude..." in a tone somewhat reminiscent of "agar Rafale hota" -- I don't think the General understands the limitations and potential of Claude. Therefore, using it as an argument that enables a very specific outcome is at best, inadvisable. In fact, the example he cites - Claude and Maven enabled Epic Fury - is a really bad example. The first night included the bombing at Minab which many now question as a Claude/Maven failing. His whole premise here is badly constructed.
9. continuing with the "if we had claude" line of thinking, that AI tools such as Claude and Maven in Indian hands would allow Hafiz Saeed to be retrieved. To be clear, in the General's mind, Hafiz Saeed would be "retrieved" in a kinetic Indian operation into Pakistan -- forget what is in reality, let's just focus on his hypothetical. A General who thinks that what's stopping such a crossing of the international border into a nuclear armed enemy that has already bested the Indian armed forces as recently as May 2025, is the lack of AI... is... well, not very clued in. And not very strategic.

I saw a lot of excitement and energy in the LTG's voice and expressions. He is part of a cadre of retired officers who, post retirement, suddenly have the whole master plan and know exactly what to do, of course, in their capacity as newly minted AI experts. But in going down this road, at least to me, the LTG betrays not only the lack of his understanding about innovation, venture and AI, but also of strategy.

“You have often heard me complain about the lavish spending of women, and of men, and not just of private citizens but magistrates, too. 

You have heard me complain that our state is plagued with two contrary vices, greed and extravagance, afflictions that have been the downfall of all great empires. 

The more the fortunes of our Republic grow and prosper with every passing day and the more our empire expands—we are now crossing into Greece and Asia, which are replete with all manner of seductive pleasures, and we are even laying hands on the treasures of kings—the more I shudder at the thought that these things may have captured us rather than we them.  

Those statues from Syracuse were enemy standards brought against the city, believe me. Already I hear all too many people praising and admiring the artifacts of Corinth and Athens, and ridiculing the earthenware antefixes of the Roman gods. But I prefer to have these gods smiling on us, and I hope they will, if we allow them to remain in their abodes.

In our fathers’ day Pyrrhus used his envoy Cineas to solicit the support not only of our men, but of our women, too, with gifts. 

The Oppian law had not yet been enacted to curtail female extravagance and even so no woman accepted the gifts. Why do you think that was? 

For the same reason that our ancestors had no need for legal sanctions in such matters—there was no extravagance to be curtailed. Just as diseases must be diagnosed before cures are found, so desires appear before the laws to curb them. 

What brought about the Licinian law of the 500 iugera but the unconscionable greed for extending one’s lands? What gave rise to the Cincian law regarding emoluments and honoraria but the fact that the commons had started to become tribute-paying subjects of the senate? 

Little wonder then that neither the Oppian nor any other law was required to limit expenditure by women at a time when women of their own accord would not accept gold and purple offered to them as gifts. 

If it were today that Cineas was doing the rounds of the city with those gifts, he would have found women standing in the streets to receive them.

And yet in the case of some appetites I, personally, cannot fathom the rhyme or reason for them. Your not being allowed something that another is allowed might cause some understandable shame or annoyance; but if everybody’s level of personal adornment is standardized, what is it that each of you fears may make her, in particular, stand out? 

The deepest embarrassment arises over penny-pinching or lack of means, but the law removes that from you in both cases when you do not have precisely what you are not allowed to have. ‘It is just this kind of leveling that I cannot tolerate,’ says the rich woman. ‘Why can I not be admired for the splendor of my gold and purple? 

Why is other women’s lack of means hidden and excused by this law, which makes it appear that they would have had, if it were lawful, just what they are unable to have?’”

text:
Movie #174 on the 2026 Popcorn Bucket List is RUNNER, the upcoming release, not be confused with Gal Gadot's THE RUNNER on @PrimeVideo.
Alan Ritchson, of Prime's REACHER, is teamed up with Owen Wilson in a buddy actioner that doesn't sizzle like his SHANGHAI NOON entries, but it competent enough to provide a decent amount of entertainment and distraction, which pretty much means success in my book.
Ritchson is Hank, a driver for a delivery side hustle that sees him picking up and delivering odds and ends, including an exotic bird that is the subject of a custody battle in an intense break-up situation. 
His contact sends him to pick up an urgent package at the airport, and he discovers that package is actually Wilson's Ben Bishop, who is delivering a package of his own - a high tech cooler containing a liver - meant for a little girl who has a very rare blood type, making organ donors pretty hard to find. 
It's not long before we discover Hank's mission was to secure that cooler, not Bishop. Turns out the matron of an international cartel shares that rare blood type and needs the liver too.
Car chases abound. Bullets rip through the air. Explosions explode. Action actions.
Ritchson is perfectly cast as Hank, a mountain of a man who used to be a Navy Seal and is just celebrating his first year of sobriety. His addiction destroyed his family and getting this liver to that little girl is VERY important to him.
Wilson is a less than perfect casting choice. For my tastes, Bishop should have been a smaller, more petite man with an annoying rapid fire delivery, like something we could have seen from Ken Jeong or Ke Huy Quan.
The movie is good-enough buddy flick that feels very much like a streaming actioner, say, along the lines of HEADS OF STATE, which was certainly enjoyable. There are lapses in logic, to be sure, but stay with it and let director Scott Waugh cook.
There is an car chase sequence in act three that is simply amazing. I'm not sure how long the single take effects had been going on before I noticed it, but Waugh's camera spends an eternity zooming in and out of car windows, through vehicles, out the back through bullet-shattered glass, back up the road between the vehicles - again and again, all while cars wreck and lots of things go boom. 
It is worth the price of admission alone. 
Is this a perfect movie, no? But, it is fairly family-friendly. It's pretty clear that when Angel Studios acquired it for distribution, the script got a scrubbing. I noticed ONE S-word in a story that could have been filled with F bombs. 
That's kind of refreshing. 
As with most Angel films, they offer a chance to buy a ticket for those who can't afford one on their own. Whether you want to take advantage of the offer, or are willing to contribute, that link is https://t.co/fO61Eb9Nzg.

We’re starting to see the premiums come back into Wagyu, particularly in the F1 market, and I think there’s a real opportunity ahead.

As feeder prices move up, bull prices generally follow, but there’s usually a lag.

For commercial producers, this could be a good opportunity to move out older, obsolete genetics and replace them with younger bulls that offer greater genetic merit and a longer working life.

Genetic gain in cattle is a slow game, so when the opportunity comes to speed it up and do it cost-effectively, I think you take it.

text:
# 🏈 Bills @ Texans — Week 1, 2026

Buffalo allowed **zero touchdowns on 61 intermediate targets** last season — and gave up the worst
rushing number in this study at 101.2 a game. Houston's answer to that is a back the market has
priced at 30.5 yards while his position room's starter sits on reserve.

> Line: BUF −1.5 · Total: 44.5 · ML: BUF −118 / HOU −102
> Implied: BUF 23.0 — HOU 21.5
> Sunday, Sept 13 · 1:00 PM ET · NRG Stadium · roof closed / astroturf · 72°F controlled
> Sean McDermott vs. DeMeco Ryans · both off 7 days

---

## Environment

Light drizzle outside, roof closed, 72 degrees on a controlled track. **No weather variable** — the
numbers below travel intact in both directions, and nothing about wind or footing argues for
suppressing the deep ball or the kicking game.

A −118 / −102 moneyline is as close to a true coin flip as the Week 1 board offers, and the 44.5
total reflects two defenses that were genuinely good in 2025 in completely different ways. This is a
game decided by which defense's specific weakness gets attacked, because both of them have exactly
one.

Roster status first, and it is decisive here:

- **Joe Mixon is on reserve.** Houston's backfield is Montgomery and Marks, and the market has not
  fully repriced it.
- **Tank Dell and Jayden Higgins are on reserve.** Nico Collins is not merely Houston's WR1, he is
  close to the entire operation, with Xavier Hutchinson and Kayshon Boutte behind him.
- **Gabe Davis and Tyrell Shavers are on reserve** for Buffalo. The receiver room is DJ Moore,
  Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman and Josh Palmer.

---

## Defenses — the yards

### Houston defense allowed / game (2025)

| Group | Yds/g | Note |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| QB pass | 201.1 | genuinely stingy |
| RB rush | **67.1** | the stoutest run defense in this entire study |
| WR rec | 105.5 | solid |
| TE rec | 40.8 | average |

Houston posted **−0.130 EPA per dropback allowed, the best mark of the eight defenses studied
here**, on a 25.9% blitz rate and a 6.96% sack rate. They do it without gambling, and the bands show
a defense with no obvious door:

| Throw depth | Targets | Comp% | Yds/target | EPA/target | TDs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Behind LOS | 63 | 69.8 | 3.0 | −0.460 | 1 |
| 0–9 | 136 | 63.2 | 5.2 | **−0.064** | 3 |
| 10–19 | 70 | 52.9 | 8.4 | +0.253 | 3 |
| 20+ | 45 | **31.1** | 9.2 | +0.193 | 3 |

That **−0.064 in the 0-to-9 band is the only negative short-zone figure in this report.** Most
defenses concede the quick game as the cost of doing business; Houston actively wins there. Combine
that with 31.1% completion allowed past twenty and 67.1 rushing yards, and you have a unit with no
cheap yards available anywhere. The intermediate is the least-bad option and it is only +0.253.

### Buffalo defense allowed / game (2025)

| Group | Yds/g | Note |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| QB pass | **175.7** | the best passing number in this study |
| RB rush | **101.2** | the worst rushing number in this study |
| WR rec | 113.6 | live |
| TE rec | **29.9** | they erase tight ends |

Buffalo generated an **8.10% sack rate — the highest of the eight** — on a 28.7% blitz rate. The
pass defense is real. The bands explain both the strength and the one true crack:

| Throw depth | Targets | Comp% | Yds/target | EPA/target | TDs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Behind LOS | 52 | 69.2 | 3.2 | −0.455 | 1 |
| 0–9 | 122 | 68.9 | 6.0 | +0.051 | 7 |
| 10–19 | 61 | 55.7 | 9.2 | +0.417 | **0** |
| 20+ | 37 | 37.8 | 10.6 | **+0.535** | 2 |

Look at the intermediate row carefully, because it is easy to misread. Buffalo gave up 9.2 yards a
target there — real yardage — and **zero touchdowns on 61 targets.** You can move the ball on
Buffalo between ten and twenty yards. You cannot score on them there. The scoring leak is split
between the quick game (seven touchdowns) and the deep shot, where the +0.535 EPA is the highest
figure Buffalo allowed anywhere.

The headline, though, is the ground. **101.2 rushing yards a game to running backs** against a
league where these eight defenses averaged well below that. It is the one place Buffalo is simply
beatable on volume.

*Both throw-depth tables come from ten charted games per defense, not seventeen.*

---

## Key players

### James Cook — RB, Buffalo
- 2025: 100.4 rush yds/g · median **107.5** · **11 of 16 over 74.5 (69%)** · L5 104.4
- One of the genuinely elite volume rushers in football, and the line at 74.5 sits 26 yards below
  his season average and 33 below his median.
- The counter-signal is real and I am not burying it: **Houston allowed 67.1 rushing yards a game to
  backs, the stiffest number in this study.** This is strength against strength, and the market's
  74.5 is an honest split of the two. What tips it is workload — 17.5 carries priced, a 69% history
  at this exact number, and a Bills team that wants to shorten a coin-flip road game.
- Projection: 75–105 yards, 16–20 carries, live for a score

### Nico Collins — WR, Houston
- 2025: 74.5 rec yds/g · median 75.0 · **8 of 15 over 69.5 (53%)** · L5 **84.0**
- Receptions: 4.7/g · median 4.0 · **4 of 15 over 5.5 (27%)** · L5 3.8
- Charting: **12.69 average target depth**, 39.6% of Houston's intended air yards, 229 targets, and
  **+1.37 yards after catch above expectation** on only 2.26 yards of separation — he wins contested,
  not open.
- With Dell and Higgins on reserve he is functionally the whole passing game, and his 12.69 aDOT sits
  in Buffalo's leakiest yardage band. But note the shape: Buffalo allowed **zero touchdowns** in the
  10-to-19 range. This is a yardage matchup, not a touchdown matchup.
- The receptions line is the tell. At 5.5 he has cleared it **four times in fifteen games.** A
  low-separation, high-aDOT receiver produces yards in chunks, not catch volume. **Over the yards,
  under the catches** is the correlated pair, and it is priced generously on both sides.
- Projection: 4–6 catches, 70–95 yards

### C.J. Stroud — QB, Houston
- 2025: 217.2 pass yds/g · median 218.0 · **7 of 14 over 218.5 (50%)** · L5 212.6
- Charting: 7.93 aDOT, −1.25 air yards to the sticks, 11.7% aggressiveness, +1.14 CPOE. Steady,
  efficient, low-variance, and utterly average in volume.
- This is the definition of a correctly priced line — a coin flip at his median, against a Buffalo
  defense allowing 175.7 that will make him earn every yard. There is no edge here and I am not going
  to invent one.
- Projection: 200–230 yards, 1–2 TD

### David Montgomery — RB, Houston
- 2025: 42.1 rush yds/g · median **32.0** · **5 of 17 over 53.5 (29%)** · L5 34.6
- The market has him at 53.5 rushing yards, which is 11 above his season average and **21 above his
  median.** He cleared this number in fewer than a third of his games last year, in a Detroit
  committee, and he is in a committee again.
- Projection: 35–55 yards — and the under is the side with the evidence

### Khalil Shakir — WR, Buffalo
- 2025: 44.9 rec yds/g · median 44.0 · **9 of 16 over 37.5 (56%)** · L5 **31.0**
- **+2.29 yards after catch above expectation** on a 3.75 aDOT with 3.86 separation — a pure
  YAC-and-separation slot who catches it at the line and creates.
- And that is the problem. His entire operating band is Houston's best band: **−0.064 EPA per target
  in the 0-to-9 range,** the only negative short-zone mark in this report. The skill is real; the
  matchup specifically neutralizes it. His last five at 31.0 already reflects some of this.
- Projection: 3–5 catches, 30–45 yards

---

## Nobody's pricing this

### Woody Marks — RB, Houston · 30.5 rushing yards

Three facts, from three different places in the database, that only mean something together.

**One: Joe Mixon is on reserve.** Not questionable, not a committee wrinkle — unavailable. Houston's
backfield is David Montgomery and Woody Marks, and nobody else with a meaningful workload.

**Two: Marks was better than his role last season.** 49.0 rushing yards a game with a **median of
55.0** and a last-five of **54.3**, and he cleared 30.5 in **9 of 14 games (64%)** — as the backup,
behind Mixon, on a snap count that was never his to control.

**Three: Buffalo allowed 101.2 rushing yards a game to running backs — the worst figure among the
eight defenses in this report.** Not soft-ish. The single most beatable run defense on this page,
attached to a pass defense so good (175.7 allowed, 8.10% sack rate) that Houston has every strategic
reason to keep the ball on the ground rather than test it.

His line is 30.5. His median last year was 55.0. The starter ahead of him is on reserve, and the
opponent is the softest run defense in the study.

The caveat worth stating: Montgomery is still nominally the lead and is priced at 13.5 carries to
Marks' 7.5, so this is a share bet, not a bell-cow bet. But at 30.5 yards Marks needs roughly four
carries at his career pace, and the anytime touchdown at **+220** is the leveraged version if
Houston's goal-line work tilts young.

---

## The simulation

**Opening drive.** Buffalo comes out committed to Cook — five carries on the opening possession, 31
yards, and a third-and-3 conversion. It stalls at the Houston 22 when the Texans' front, which gave
up the fewest rushing yards in this study, finally holds on second-and-2. Field goal, 3–0 Bills.

**Q1.** Houston answers with the plan the numbers demand: Marks and Montgomery alternate, and the
Bills' run defense yields exactly what it yielded all last season. A twelve-play drive, nine of them
runs, ends with Marks converting from three yards out. 7–3 Texans.

**Q2.** Josh Allen finds the deep band — Buffalo's own scouting report on Houston says the
intermediate is the only door, but Allen's 6.86 average target depth means he takes what's given: a
Shakir screen, a Kincaid seam, a Cook check-down. It produces a field goal, not a touchdown, and
that distinction is the game. Houston's next drive is a Collins showcase — two contested wins for 41
combined yards — before a Buffalo sack on second-and-8 kills it. Field goal. **Halftime: 10–9
Houston.**

**Q3.** The Bills' 8.10% sack rate finally shows up. Stroud goes down twice on the opening drive of
the half, Houston punts from its own 14, and Buffalo takes over in plus territory. Cook does the
rest — three carries, then a one-yard plunge. 16–10 Buffalo. Houston answers with Marks again, and
the drive reaches the Bills' 30 before a third-down incompletion. Field goal. 16–13.

**Q4.** Buffalo tries to close it on the ground and can't — Houston's front stiffens, and the punt
gives the Texans the ball with 6:12 and a chance. Collins converts a third-and-11 on a contested
back-shoulder. But the drive dies at the Buffalo 24 on a fourth-and-2 stuff, and Cook converts two
first downs to end it.

> ### 🏆 Final: Bills 19 — Texans 16
> MVP: James Cook · Turning point: the two third-quarter sacks that flipped the field
> Swing factor: Houston's backfield without Joe Mixon — it kept them in it
> Total: 35, under 44.5

---

## Best props

*Discipline note: no algorithm grade exists for an upcoming week, and that is fine — the measured
history says a "LEAN" tier grade has hit 42.9% across 466 reconciled props. Every call below traces
to a pulled number.*

**Tier A**

- **OVER Woody Marks 30.5 rushing yards (−114)** — line 30.5 · avg 49.0 · median **55.0** ·
  **9 of 14 (64%)** · L5 54.3 · Mixon on reserve, Buffalo allows a study-worst 101.2.
- **UNDER Nico Collins 5.5 receptions (−135)** — **4 of 15 over (27%)** · avg 4.7 · L5 3.8 · a
  2.26-separation, 12.69-aDOT profile does not produce catch volume.
- **UNDER David Montgomery 53.5 rushing yards (−114)** — **5 of 17 over (29%)** · median **32.0** ·
  L5 34.6. The line sits 21 yards above his median.

**Tier B**

- **OVER James Cook 74.5 rushing yards (−114)** — avg 100.4 · median 107.5 · **11 of 16 (69%)** ·
  L5 104.4. Priced honestly against a 67.1 run defense; the volume is what carries it.
- **OVER Nico Collins 69.5 receiving yards (−114)** — avg 74.5 · median 75.0 · L5 **84.0** ·
  12.69 aDOT into Buffalo's 9.2-yards-per-target intermediate band.
- **UNDER DJ Moore 47.5 receiving yards (−114)** — **6 of 17 over (35%)** · avg 40.1 · L5 36.0.
- **UNDER Khalil Shakir 37.5 receiving yards (−114)** — L5 31.0, and his 3.75-aDOT YAC game runs
  directly into the only negative short-zone EPA figure in this report.

**Darts**

- Dart: Woody Marks anytime TD (+220) — the leveraged version of the Tier A call.
- Dart: James Cook anytime TD (−105) — goal-line back for a favorite.
- Dart: Dalton Schultz OVER 33.5 receiving yards (−114) — 10 of 17, avg 45.7, L5 45.0. The caution:
  Buffalo allowed a study-best 29.9 tight end yards a game, so this is form against matchup.

**Game: UNDER 44.5.** Two defenses with genuine strengths, a 72-degree controlled track that
produces no chaos, and two quarterbacks averaging under 8.0 air yards a throw.

---

## The Stack

**Safe — the ground game decides a coin-flip game.**
Buffalo's one weakness is the run and Houston's one weakness is the run, so both backfields eat while
the passing games grind against good coverage. That script caps the total and the receptions.

- OVER Woody Marks 30.5 rush yds · UNDER Nico Collins 5.5 receptions · UNDER 44.5

**Lotto — Houston's backfield actually breaks the game open.**
Mixon's absence forces volume onto two backs against the softest run defense here; if Houston leans
all the way in, Marks gets the goal line and Collins gets the play-action shots that follow.

- Marks anytime TD · OVER Marks 30.5 rush · OVER Collins 69.5 rec yds · UNDER Josh Allen 220.5 pass

---

## More angles

- **UNDER Dalton Kincaid 38.5 receiving yards (−114)** — L5 **25.0** against a season average of
  47.5. The recent form and the matchup agree; Houston allows 40.8 to tight ends but Kincaid's role
  shrank down the stretch.
- **OVER Josh Allen 30.5 rushing yards (−116)** — a constant even in a run-first plan, and Buffalo
  will be protecting a lead in the fourth.
- **Fade: any Houston deep-shot prop.** Buffalo allowed 37.8% completion past twenty. Collins gets
  his yards in the intermediate, not over the top.
- **Nico Collins anytime TD (+160) is the one Collins market I'd avoid** — Buffalo allowed **zero
  touchdowns on 61 intermediate targets**, which is precisely where he lives. The yards transfer; the
  score does not.
- **Game flow to watch:** Buffalo's 8.10% sack rate is the highest in this study and Houston's line
  has to hold up without a run game threat if they fall behind. Two sacks on one drive is how this
  game gets decided, and it is how the Under cashes.

---

Buffalo can't stop the run and can't be scored on in the middle. Houston can't be run on and can't
be thrown deep. Both teams' best players are pointed at the other's strength — so does this come
down to Woody Marks?
